analysis.one_liner: Lets regulators block, detain, or destroy imported food that could make people sick, and adds inspectors.
analysis.headline: The food-safety bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on May 26, 1999 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require imported food to be produced under safety rules that meet U.S. standards or an equivalent system. It would let the government deny entry to foods tied to repeated disease outbreaks, detain shipments until they are cleared, destroy dangerous food at the importer's expense, ban repeat-offender importers, and double the bond required of violators. It would also fund more FDA inspectors and CDC grants to state health departments for tracking foodborne illness.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who eat imported food, which is a large share of the American food supply. The bill also benefits state and local health departments, which would get federal grants to detect and investigate foodborne disease outbreaks.

how_it_helps.text: Requires all imported food to be prepared, packed, and held under a system meeting U.S. requirements, or one the Secretary of Health and Human Services certifies as equivalent, with systematic evaluations of foreign food systems.

Creates a system to deny entry to foods from a specific producer, shipper, growing area, or country that has been repeatedly adulterated or repeatedly tied to foodborne disease outbreaks, with an emergency path for a single serious outbreak.

Lets the Secretary bar distribution of imported food until it is authorized, require secure storage, order destruction of dangerous food at the owner's expense, label refused food 'United States: Refused Entry,' and treat 'port shopping' (re-offering previously refused food without proving compliance) as adulteration.
Authorizes debarment of people who repeatedly or deliberately import adulterated food or commit food-import felonies, and doubles to a sliding scale the customs bond for importers with violations.
Authorizes funding for additional FDA laboratory, inspection, and compliance personnel for fiscal years 2000-2002.

Directs the CDC to make grants to state and local health departments for surveillance and prevention of foodborne disease, funds pathogen-detection research, and supports training and public information.

analysis.who_pays: Food importers and the foreign producers they buy from, who would bear the cost of equivalent production systems, detention and secure storage, destruction of refused shipments, higher bonds, and the risk of being barred from the U.S. market. Some of that cost would likely show up in food prices.

drawbacks.text: Importers and foreign producers would bear real compliance costs, and small importers would face the same detention, storage, and destruction requirements as large ones, with those costs partly passed to consumers through prices.

The bill requires denial-of-entry determinations to be made in a manner consistent with U.S. bilateral, regional, and multilateral trade agreements, so trade obligations could limit how aggressively the government blocks imports even under the new authority.

Denial-of-entry determinations include a process for affected parties to submit comments, and a denial lapses if the government fails to act on remediation evidence within 90 days, which critics could point to as opportunities for delay by repeat violators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is protection from contaminated imports at a time when foodborne illness from imported produce and seafood was a documented concern, paid for mainly by importers through compliance costs rather than by taxpayers directly, since new FDA positions and CDC grants were separately authorized. The design is fairly targeted: it focuses on repeat offenders and specific violators rather than blanket restrictions, and it builds in comment and remediation processes for affected importers. The main honest objection is cost pass-through to consumers and the possibility that trade-agreement obligations blunt the enforcement powers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, so it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Barbara Mikulski introduced the bill on May 26, 1999, joined by Sens. Kennedy and Durbin; both signed on as cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House action before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food importers and foreign food producers are better off, because they avoided new detention, bonding, destruction, and debarment requirements; consumers gained nothing, since the safety rules never took effect.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Mikulski
for.role: U.S. Senator from Maryland, lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Imported Food Safety Improvement Act of 1999 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Edward Kennedy and Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senators from Massachusetts and Illinois, cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it three Democratic Senate supporters in total.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for food and agriculture legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 26, 1999 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape can only be inferred: the three supporters were all Democrats, and the bill sat untouched in a committee run by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would let regulators halt distribution of imported food until cleared, require secure storage and destruction at the importer's expense, double bonds for violators, and debar repeat offenders. Its enforcement costs fall directly on this industry, which is why weaker oversight of imports is in its interest.

Imported food would have to meet U.S. standards or certified equivalents, and foods from specific producers, growing areas, or countries tied to repeated outbreaks could be denied entry entirely. Market access would become conditional on food-safety performance.

The bill authorizes CDC grants and technical assistance to state and local health agencies for foodborne disease surveillance, investigation, and prevention, particularly for illnesses linked to imported food.
